meta.title: Who really said "Here I stand; I can do no other. God help me. Amen"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Disputed: no Diet transcript or eyewitness records Luther saying "Here I stand" at Worms in 1521. The words appear in early printed reports of his speech.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Here I stand; I can do no other. God help me. Amen'?
meta.ogDescription: Luther's Worms speech ended "God help me. Amen." The famous "Here I stand" is in early printed reports, not the Diet transcripts. Scholars doubt he said it.

answer.label: Disputed — probably added to Luther’s speech in print
answer.sourceLine: Luther did end his reply at the Diet of Worms (18 April 1521) with “God help me. Amen.” The words “Here I stand; I can do no other” are not in the Diet transcripts or eyewitness accounts. They first appear in printed reports of the speech, and most scholars doubt he spoke them. The English wording is a later translation.

source.heading: What the earliest reports actually say

No single source. Thomas Mall’s 1665 Sufferers Mirrour was the first English rendering of the Worms line as “Here I stand” (per Young)

source.excerpt: Ich kan nicht anderst, hie[r] stehe ich, Gott helff mir, Amen.
trail: Wikiquote lists “Hier stehe ich, ich kann nicht anders” in its Disputed section ↗. It says the words have no sign in the Diet transcripts or eyewitness accounts, and that most scholars now doubt they were spoken.

Samuel L. Young’s Lutheran Quarterly study ↗ gives the early forms. A Strasbourg account has only “GOTT HELF MIR ARMEN. Amen.” The standard report has “Ich kan nicht anderst, hie[r] stehe ich, Gott helff mir, Amen.”

Scott H. Hendrix, quoted by Elesha Coffman in Christianity Today (2002) ↗: “The earliest printed version of Luther’s address added these words, which were not recorded on the spot.” He adds that “for almost a half-century now, most scholars have believed they were probably not spoken by Luther.”
The German reference site wissen.de ↗ says the line was not spoken at Worms. It says the version printed in Wittenberg sharpened the ending, and that nobody knows who made the change.
source.excerptNote: The line as Samuel L. Young transcribes it from the “more standard report on the Diet” (Weimar edition 7:838). Word for word it reads “I can do no other, here I stand, God help me, Amen” (quotle’s literal gloss). In that report “here I stand” comes after “I can do no other.” Young also reports that a Strasbourg account printed the following month has only “GOTT HELF MIR ARMEN. Amen.”

sourceLink.text: Samuel L. Young, “How Luther Became the Mythical ‘Here I Stand’ Hero,” Lutheran Quarterly (Spring 2022)

source.useLine: The 1521 German report and early English renderings of it are public domain, but this exact English wording can’t be traced to one translation, so we give no rights status. Credit it as shown above — just don’t present this wording as public domain.
source.rightsNote: The German report of the speech dates from 1521 and has long been in the public domain. English renderings such as “Here I stand: I can do no otherwise: God help me! Amen” (Arminian Magazine, 1778, per Young ↗) are old enough to be free. But this exact wording, “I can do no other,” could not be traced to one specific translation, so quotle.info asserts no rights status for it.

author.name: Martin Luther
author.heading: About Martin Luther
author.metaLine: 1483–1546 · German theologian & leader of the Protestant Reformation
author.bio: Martin Luther (10 November 1483 – 18 February 1546) was the German friar and theologian whose challenge to the papacy began the Protestant Reformation. In April 1521 he was summoned before Emperor Charles V at the Diet of Worms, where he refused to recant his writings. The scene became the most retold moment of his life, and “Here I stand” became its shorthand.

misattribution.heading: Where the famous line came from
misattribution.intro: The speech is real and so is its ending, “God help me. Amen.” What is disputed is the defiant clause in front of it. It appears in printed reports of the speech, but not in any record taken on the spot.

items.scope: “Here I stand; I can do no other”
items.why: Scott H. Hendrix, quoted by Elesha Coffman in Christianity Today ↗, says the earliest printed version “added these words, which were not recorded on the spot.” wissen.de ↗ says the Wittenberg print sharpened the ending and that no one knows who did it.

Wikiquote ↗ notes that Diarmaid MacCulloch, in Reformation: Europe’s House Divided (2003), traces the quotation to Georg Rörer, the editor of Luther’s collected works, who wanted to add a summary of Luther’s statement.

Young ↗ traces the English. Foxe (1583) has “Hereupon I stand and rest.” Thomas Mall’s 1665 Sufferers Mirrour was the first English rendering of the Worms line as “Here I stand.” John Wesley’s Arminian Magazine (April 1778) gives “Here I stand: I can do no otherwise: God help me! Amen.”

As quoted on bredenhof.ca ↗, Bainton’s Here I Stand (p. 185) argues that the words, “though not recorded on the spot, may nevertheless be genuine,” because “the listeners at the moment may have been too moved to write.”

misattribution.truthLine: Luther really did close with “God help me. Amen.” The “Here I stand” clause is not in the Diet transcripts or eyewitness accounts, and Wikiquote ↗ classes it as disputed.

context.heading: Why the line stuck
lead: At Worms on 18 April 1521, Luther refused to recant unless he was convinced by Scripture or clear reason. Wikiquote ↗ gives the documented close in Karl Heim’s translation: “I cannot and will not recant anything, since it is neither safe nor right to go against conscience. May God help me. Amen.”

The shorter, punchier “Here I stand” won out anyway. According to Young ↗, Roland Bainton “immortalized the line in the mid-twentieth century by using it as the title of his classic biography of the Reformer.”
